tldr: Rather than learning individual muscle activations directly, this work uses reinforcement learning at runtime to modulate just four key gains and thresholds of a fixed reflex controller via residual modulation, achieving both human-like natural walking and robust adaptability to muscle weakness and external perturbations in a musculoskeletal model.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed Residual-Reflex RL framework. The fixed, phase-dependent reflex controller shown in the lower part handles the base muscle coordination, while the reinforcement learning (MPO) policy in the upper part outputs only four residual parameters to modulate reflex gains and thresholds in real time according to the current state.
overview:
Walking simulation with muscle-driven musculoskeletal models is attracting significant attention as a foundation for biomechanical analysis and generating realistic animations. However, producing natural, physiologically plausible walking like a human while maintaining flexible adaptability to muscle weakness and external pushes has long been an extremely difficult challenge.

Existing approaches have largely fallen into two categories. One is embedding biological motor control rules directly, such as reflex controllers. While these reliably produce human-like movements, their fixed parameters prevent them from adapting to unexpected environmental changes or muscle weakness. The other approach is using deep reinforcement learning (RL) to learn all muscle excitations directly from scratch. Although this offers high adaptability, the policy must discover muscle coordination patterns from scratch in a high-dimensional, redundant muscle space, which often leads to unnatural joint motions and ground reaction forces.

To address this, the authors focused on the fact that biological systems do not control muscles in isolation; instead, they leverage existing neuromuscular mechanisms such as spinal reflexes. Rather than learning reflex mechanisms again from scratch, they asked: why not let reinforcement learning fine-tune the behavior of an already established reflex controller according to the situation?

Specifically, they developed "Residual-Reflex RL," a framework built upon a gait-phase-dependent reflex circuit where an RL policy (using the MPO algorithm) modulates only four biomechanically critical reflex parameters in real time, governing hip swing, knee support, and ankle propulsion.

Experimental results show that during nominal walking, the proposed method achieves joint kinematics and ground reaction forces that closely match human reference data, greatly outperforming existing direct-learning methods in bilateral symmetry and stride-to-stride consistency. Furthermore, without any retraining, the model autonomously slows its walking speed to maintain stability under ankle muscle weakness (reduced soleus strength) and successfully recovers its balance from a 100 N torso push perturbation.
contributions: Reformulated reinforcement learning from a task of directly controlling individual muscles into a task of state-dependent modulation of an existing neuromuscular reflex mechanism.

Introduced a compact, interpretable learning interface that adjusts reflex pathways using just four-dimensional residual parameters directly linked to primary walking functions (leg swing, knee support, and ankle propulsion).

Demonstrated high consistency with human kinematic data (joint trajectories) and dynamic data (vertical ground reaction forces), along with superior stride-to-stride repeatability and bilateral symmetry in nominal walking.
Showed that the same learned policy flexibly adapts to soleus muscle weakness (up to a 17% reduction) and strong external impact perturbations (100 N) without any retraining.

sections.heading: Modulating Reflex Effectiveness Rather Than Learning Muscles Directly
sections.summary: Balancing physiological plausibility with adaptability to environmental and muscular changes has long been a challenge in muscle-driven locomotion. This work proposes an approach that avoids direct control of 18 muscles, instead using reinforcement learning to modulate four key parameters of a fixed reflex controller in real time.
sections.details:
Unlike models that specify joint torques directly, musculoskeletal simulations give rise to natural motion through the interplay of neural excitation, muscle-tendon complex dynamics, and environmental contact. However, achieving both physiological plausibility (human-likeness) and adaptability to external disturbances or muscle capacity changes has been remarkably difficult.

Conventional approaches have typically relied on either biologically informed structured controllers (such as reflex controllers or CPGs) or direct muscle excitation control via deep reinforcement learning. The former produces human-like motion but lacks adaptability due to fixed parameters, whereas the latter offers adaptability but explores a high-dimensional, redundant muscle space from scratch, frequently settling into unnatural gait patterns.

Looking at biological motor control, humans do not control muscles individually; they achieve coordinated movement through sensory feedback and spinal reflexes. Therefore, rather than forcing reinforcement learning to rediscover muscle synergies from scratch, it is more natural to let it adjust the parameters of existing reflex circuits according to the situation.

Based on this insight, the paper proposes "Reflex-Informed Neuromuscular Reinforcement Learning," which builds upon a fixed reflex controller while using an RL policy to modulate four critical reflex gains and thresholds governing hip swing, knee support, and ankle propulsion in a state-dependent manner.

sections.heading: Bridging Structured Neuromuscular Control and Deep Reinforcement Learning
sections.summary: Locomotion control research is broadly divided into bio-inspired methods such as reflex control and muscle synergies, and end-to-end muscle control using deep RL. This work establishes a new middle ground by combining the strengths of both, adjusting fixed reflex circuits in real time with reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
### Musculoskeletal Character Simulation
Musculoskeletal simulations using Hill-type muscle-tendon models have been widely used in biomechanics to analyze normal and pathological gait and evaluate the effects of aging and impairments. In recent years, they have also been adopted in computer graphics animation, serving as a solid foundation for physically plausible motion generation.

### Structured Neuromuscular Control
Central pattern generators (CPGs), muscle synergies, and reflex controllers are prominent methods for directly modeling biological motor control laws. In particular, the reflex controller by Geyer et al. is renowned for reproducing stable human walking by computing muscle stimulation directly from sensory feedback such as muscle length and force. However, these rely on manual design or offline optimization, leaving control parameters fixed during execution and making dynamic adaptation to muscle weakness or unexpected environmental changes difficult.

### Muscle Control via Reinforcement Learning
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) provides high adaptability by learning muscle activations directly through interaction with the environment. Numerous enhancements have been introduced, such as DEP-RL to improve exploration efficiency, biomimetic rewards, and integrating CPGs with learned reflex networks. Nonetheless, methods that directly output muscle activations still suffer from the tendency to produce unnatural gaits that deviate from human kinematics and ground reaction force characteristics.

sections.heading: How Four-Dimensional Residual Actions Drive Reflex Parameters
sections.summary: Using a 9-degree-of-freedom, 18-muscle musculoskeletal model, the authors built a gait-phase-dependent reflex controller. The reinforcement learning policy (MPO) takes a 121-dimensional state and outputs just four-dimensional residual actions, modulating key reflex gains and thresholds in real time to derive full-body muscle excitations.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Framework Overview
The system consists of a musculoskeletal simulator, a phase-dependent reflex controller, and an RL policy that outputs residual actions (Figure F1). It adopts Maximum a Posteriori Policy Optimization (MPO), an off-policy RL algorithm, to ensure stable policy updates.

### 3.2 Musculoskeletal Model
The simulation uses Hyfydy with the sagittal-plane human model "H0918v2j" (Figure F2). It is a 9-degree-of-freedom model comprising the pelvis, torso, and the thighs, shanks, and feet of both legs, actuated by nine muscle groups per side (a total of 18 Hill-type muscle-tendon units). Spherical contact elements are placed at the heel and toes of each foot, and the control loop updates every 0.005 seconds.

### 3.3 Neuromuscular Control Mechanism
The reflex controller receives muscle length and velocity feedback modeling muscle spindles, muscle force feedback modeling Golgi tendon organs, and torso pitch angle feedback. The gait cycle is divided into five phases (early stance, late stance, lift-off, swing, and landing preparation), switching active feedback pathways depending on the phase.

### 3.4 Residual Neuromuscular Regulation
The action space of the policy is only four-dimensional ($\mathbf{a}_t \in \mathbb{R}^4$). Parameters are dynamically adjusted relative to nominal values $p_{i,0}$ using a modulation scaling factor $\lambda = 0.5$ via $p_i(t) = p_{i,0}(1 + \lambda a_i(t))$. The four selected parameters are:
- $a_1$: Muscle length gain of the hamstrings (HAM) during swing (modulating hip extension and knee flexion)
- $a_2$: Muscle length threshold of the iliopsoas (ILI) during stance (modulating hip flexion and the initiation of forward leg swing)
- $a_3$: Muscle force gain of the soleus (SOL) across all phases (modulating ankle support and push-off propulsion)
- $a_4$: Muscle force gain of the monoarticular knee extensors (VAS) during stance (enhancing knee support)

### 3.5 Reinforcement Learning via MPO
The observation vector $\mathbf{s}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{121}$ includes muscle fiber lengths, velocities, and forces, muscle excitations and activations, foot positions, and joint angles and angular velocities. The reward function focuses on target speed tracking as the primary objective, penalized for excessive contact forces, sudden excitation changes, unnecessary muscle effort, joint limit violations, pelvis tilt and center-of-mass sway, and the rate of parameter change.

captions.F2: The musculoskeletal model H0918v2j used in the experiments (a) and the layout of the nine pairs of modeled muscle-tendon units (18 in total) (b). Monoarticular and biarticular muscles coordinate to actuate the hip, knee, and ankle joints.

sections.heading: Remarkably Human-Like Walking and Superior Adaptation to Weakness and Pushes
sections.summary: The method was evaluated across three experiments: nominal walking (0.8, 1.0, 1.2 m/s), soleus muscle weakness, and backward push perturbations. The proposed method outperformed baselines in kinematic/dynamic human-likeness, gait symmetry, and stride consistency, and withstood muscle weakness and 100 N perturbations without retraining.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Evaluation Protocol and Baselines
Baselines included "E2E-RL" which directly outputs muscle excitations, "DEP-RL" with improved exploration, and a fixed reflex controller whose reflex parameters were optimized offline using CMA-ES.

### 4.2 Evaluation on Nominal Walking
- Velocity tracking: The proposed method tracked target speeds with high precision across all velocities (0.8, 1.0, 1.2 m/s), exhibiting velocity errors of only 0.01 to 0.05 m/s.
- Joint kinematic score: Evaluating agreement with human reference trajectories, the proposed method averaged 88.0%, substantially exceeding the baselines (E2E-RL: 39.0–81.9%, DEP-RL: 40.8–58.5%) (Figure F3). Kinematic fidelity at the knee and ankle improved dramatically.
- Dynamic score (Vertical Ground Reaction Force: GRF): In matching the human bimodal loading pattern, the proposed method achieved high scores of 76.7–89.8% across all speeds (Figure F7). In contrast, DEP-RL produced excessive impact peaks at initial contact and dropped to 0% at higher speeds.
- Symmetry and stride consistency: Measuring bilateral waveform errors and coefficient of variation (CV) for stride time and stride length, the proposed method maintained highly stable periodic walking with a stride time CV of 0.70% and stride length CV of 0.74% at 1.2 m/s—both well below 1% (Figure F8).

### 4.3 Adaptation to Soleus Muscle Weakness
The isometric maximum muscle force of the soleus was reduced to 83% of its nominal value, and the same policy trained at 1.2 m/s was evaluated without retraining. While the fixed reflex CMA-ES baseline quickly fell in the weakened model, the proposed method completed 25-second walking bouts across all conditions. The actual speed naturally decreased from 1.20 m/s to 0.95 m/s, and the policy autonomously increased the knee extensor gain ($a_4$) to compensate for the soleus deficit ($a_3$), closely mirroring compensatory strategies observed in humans with muscle weakness.

### 4.4 Recovery from External Push Perturbations
Experiments applied backward impulse perturbations of 75 N and 100 N to the torso for 0.1 seconds. The CMA-ES model lost balance and fell around 4.5 seconds, whereas the proposed method quickly recovered its stride and continued walking for 25 seconds even after a single 100 N pulse. It also completed 25 seconds under repeated 75 N pushes applied every 5 seconds, demonstrating strong robustness.

captions.F3: Comparison of joint kinematic scores across target walking speeds. The proposed method (blue) achieves the highest scores at all speeds, reproducing trajectories remarkably close to human data, especially at the knee and ankle, which have historically been challenging for reinforcement learning.
captions.F7: Vertical ground reaction force (GRF) profiles across target speeds. Gray bands represent the human reference range. The proposed method (bottom row) traces the characteristic smooth, bimodal human pattern, whereas E2E-RL and DEP-RL show unnatural impact spikes at initial contact and large variability.
captions.F8: Comparison of bilateral gait asymmetry error (top, lower is more symmetric) and coefficient of variation (CV) for stride time and stride length (bottom, lower is more periodic and stable). The proposed method (blue) is distinctly lower across all metrics, maintaining consistent, steady walking.

sections.heading: Why Modulating Just Four Parameters Yields Such Dramatic Improvements
sections.summary: Because the reflex circuit constrains fundamental muscle coordination patterns, reinforcement learning is freed from searching high-dimensional muscle space and can focus solely on critical state adaptation. This is the core reason behind achieving both human-likeness and environmental adaptability.
sections.details:
The experimental results demonstrate that positioning reinforcement learning as a "tuner of existing neuromuscular control mechanisms" rather than forcing it to learn muscle control from scratch is exceptionally effective.

In end-to-end direct learning, coordinated actions across 18 muscles must be discovered relying solely on task rewards (such as forward speed). Consequently, even if the task is accomplished, the gait often becomes biomechanically abnormal, exhibiting hyperextended knees or unnatural heel-strike impacts.

In the proposed framework, biomechanically meaningful muscle coordination pathways are predefined by the reflex controller. Reinforcement learning only needs to fine-tune four critical parameters according to the state. This substantially compresses the search space, enabling flexible adaptation to circumstances without compromising physiological plausibility.

The difference from offline-optimized controllers like CMA-ES is also clear. Fixed parameters cannot cope with unexpected muscle weakness or external impacts, but the RL policy in the proposed method continuously monitors the current state (such as muscle length and torso pitch) and updates residual parameters in real time, autonomously generating recovery motions to prevent falls.

sections.heading: Toward Next-Generation Muscle-Driven RL Informed by Neuroscience
sections.summary: This work establishes a new methodology using a reflex controller as a foundation and reinforcement learning as a residual modulator. Demonstrating human-like motion generation in nominal walking and strong adaptability to muscle weakness and perturbations, it holds promise for biomimetic robot control and animation technologies.
sections.details:
This study presented Reflex-Informed Neuromuscular RL, achieving both physiological plausibility and adaptability in muscle-driven locomotion. Instead of directly generating 18-dimensional muscle excitations, the framework applies residual modulation to four key biomechanical parameters of a gait-phase-dependent reflex controller.

Experiments in the Hyfydy simulator confirmed kinematics and dynamics that closely match human data, along with superior bilateral symmetry and stride-to-stride stability. Furthermore, the same trained policy demonstrated robustness by adapting to soleus muscle weakness and torso push perturbations without any retraining.

Future work includes extending the approach to continuous speed transitions involving acceleration and deceleration, more diverse musculoskeletal morphologies, and complex physical interactions such as uneven terrain locomotion and stair climbing.

takeaways: A hierarchical design that lets domain-knowledge reflex circuits handle muscle coordination while tasking RL with tuning a few meta-parameters is far more effective than solving high-dimensional muscle actuation entirely with RL.
Compressing the action space from 18-dimensional muscle excitations to just 4-dimensional reflex gains and thresholds dramatically boosts both exploration efficiency and motion human-likeness.
Modulating reflex parameters online allows compensatory gait under muscle weakness and recovery from external perturbations to emerge naturally without any additional training.

The results suggest that layering a lightweight learning-based adaptation layer over fixed-gain reflex controllers is a compelling architecture for legged robot control and rehabilitative assistive devices.
limitations: Simulations are restricted to the sagittal plane (2D), so effectiveness regarding lateral balance and turning maneuvers in 3D locomotion remains unverified.
The four modulated reflex parameters were selected manually based on biomechanical domain knowledge; automated selection and task-dependent scaling methods have not yet been established.
Evaluated walking speeds were limited to the range of 0.8 to 1.2 m/s, leaving continuous acceleration/deceleration and transitions to running as future work.
